question: Finished work on the engine is sitting on this machine and nowhere else. Three sets of written notes from earlier today have never been sent to the shared copy, and the level edits I am about to fold in will add more. I have been holding rather than sending, because sending is the point where other people and the other tools can see and build on it, and I would rather you set that policy than assume it.

options.name: Let me send finished work up whenever it is done
options.what: Once a piece of work builds clean and the tests pass, it goes to the shared copy without asking you. You stop being interrupted for it.
options.costs: Nothing of your time. Work reaches the shared copy before you have looked at it, so if you dislike something you are reverting it there instead of catching it here.

options.name: Ask you each time
options.what: Nothing leaves this machine until you say so for that specific batch.
options.costs: One short message from you a few times a day, and the work waits in between.

options.name: Keep everything local for now
options.what: Nothing is sent at all until you revisit this.
options.costs: Free today. Every finished piece exists in exactly one place, so a lost machine is a lost week, and the other tools keep reading an older version of this engine than the one I am working on.

recommend.because: Everything I would send has already been through the full build and the whole test suite before it goes, so the review you would be doing at that moment is one the machine has already done. The live risk is the other direction: your own level edits have been sitting unsaved for four days and three sets of notes for one day, all in a single copy.

detail: Three docs-only commits sit unpushed on aeon master: 3e30ccdd, d67730ed, d77137fc (2026-08-23 04:15 to 04:19 EDT). origin/master is at 139995f2. The STRAND parcel will add two data commits plus a sigil-side repin and refreeze that must be pushed as a pair with them. Empyrean attempted to consolidate this suite-wide and then agreed a hub relay cannot carry an authorization.

question: Your level edits from the nineteenth and twentieth of this month, the painting you did in the editor and the collision shapes under it, were never saved into the project history. They are loose in the working copy and have been for four days. Folding them in also means rebuilding the game and re-checking the frozen size records our assembler keeps, because level data is baked into the cartridge image. That is what I would start on, and I want to know if you would rather I started somewhere else.

options.name: Fold in my level edits first
options.what: Your painting and collision work becomes part of the project history and is safe. The game gets rebuilt and re-verified around it.
options.costs: A couple of hours, most of it me waiting on builds and the test suite. Nothing else on my list is waiting behind it.

options.name: Do the small toolchain change first
options.what: A short alignment change our assembler asked for goes in ahead of everything else.
options.costs: Under an hour of work, but it needs a fresh toolchain build before it will even read the source, and your level edits stay loose the whole time.

options.name: Push on the effects work instead
options.what: I carry on with the half that still stands between an effect you build in the editor and that effect actually running in the game.
options.costs: A day or more before there is anything to see, and your level edits stay loose the whole time.

recommend.because: It is the only thing on my list where your own work is currently unprotected, it is the shortest of the three, and it clears the ground for the other two rather than competing with them.

detail: 39 modified files in the aeon working tree, re-verified this boot: 38 data files (6 editor saves 2026-08-19/08-20 plus the 32-file re-bake they triggered) plus docs/lane-status.json. Plan and full provenance in docs/superpowers/notes/2026-08-22-dirty-tree-triage.md, commits 1 and 2, exact paths, must land together because the collision tables are interned against the strip indices. Carries the byte-changing ritual: canonical build both shapes, then repin and refreeze --ab against sigil.

question: The background art fills every tile slot it has, so the editor cannot add an animated band to it. Should this lane make a simplified test-only background to free room, or does that belong to the editor lane? There may also be a third answer where nobody needs to make art at all.

options.what: Ask the editor lane first whether a band can be made by reusing tiles the art already has
options.costs: One message and a short wait. If the answer is yes, no art work is needed by anyone and the whole question goes away. If no, you have lost an hour and still choose between the two below.

options.what: This lane makes a simplified test-only background
options.costs: A few hours here, and the picture gets plainer for testing only - your shipped art is untouched and this is inside the permission you already gave. It unblocks the editor lane without them waiting on anyone.

options.what: The editor lane makes it
options.costs: They own the art tools and would likely do a better-looking job, but they are the lane currently blocked, so they would be unblocking themselves and it lands behind their other work.

recommend: Ask the editor lane first whether a band can be made by reusing tiles the art already has
because: Our own notes say promotion - reusing existing tiles, adding none - is a working route, and it is the only option that might cost nobody any art work at all. It is one message against a few hours, and it cannot make the other two choices worse. If it comes back no, I would then recommend this lane doing it, because they are the lane that is stuck.

question: The background art has no room for an animated band. d-4 asked you to pick which lane does the art work - that was the wrong question and I am withdrawing it. Our own notes say YOU generate this art with your constrained generator and judge it by eye, so the art step is not a lane's to take. There may also be a route where no new art is needed at all. Do you want to regenerate now, or wait to hear whether that route works?

options.what: Wait for the answer on whether a band can reuse tiles the art already has
options.costs: A short wait. If it works, nothing needs regenerating and you spend no time at all. The editor lane is being asked now, so the answer should not be long.

options.what: Regenerate the background now with 320 as the generator's limit, without waiting
options.costs: Your time at the generator, plus a look on screen to judge it. It removes the uncertainty immediately and cannot be wasted - the extra room is useful either way. But if the reuse route works, you spent that time for nothing.

options.what: Leave it entirely until you next feel like touching the art
options.costs: Costs nothing now, and nothing here is urgent. The effects work stays finished-but-unproven until an animated band exists somewhere, so the first real end-to-end test keeps waiting.

recommend: Wait for the answer on whether a band can reuse tiles the art already has
because: It is the only option that might cost you nothing, the question is already being asked, and none of the other choices get worse for waiting. Worth saying plainly: the 320 figure is not a target anyone needs you to hit exactly - your own instruction was that it just has to still look slightly reasonable, and the number was picked to be generous and tightened later rather than squeezed.

question: An animated background band is stored in a slot whose size was fixed back when no act had one, and a real band needs about four thousand times that. Fixing the slot is easy; the question is how big to make it. A band's size depends entirely on how big an author draws it, and the legal range runs from 302 bytes to about 112 KB - a 380x spread. Whatever we pick, an author who draws a bigger band than that gets a build failure, so this is really a question about how much background animation you want to be possible without an engine change.

options.name: Pick a generous ceiling now and refuse politely above it
options.what: We reserve room for a band up to 16 tiles wide by 8 tall - about eight times the one Aurora just drew, and comfortably inside the spare room that already exists next to it. Anything bigger stops the build with a message naming the limit, instead of the cryptic collision we get today. Authors never think about this again until they hit the ceiling.
options.costs: About 32 KB of cartridge space set aside whether or not an act uses it. You have roughly 350 KB spare, so it is not tight. If you ever want a band bigger than that, raising it is a small change but it is a change.

options.name: Reserve enough for the biggest band that could ever exist
options.what: Room for a band covering every tile the background has. No author can ever hit a limit, and this question never comes back.
options.costs: About 112 KB set aside permanently, which is very nearly all the spare room in that part of the cartridge. It would leave that neighbourhood with almost nothing left for anything else later.

options.name: Re-measure the layout every time the band changes size
options.what: No space is wasted and no ceiling exists. The layout is recomputed to fit whatever the author actually drew.
options.costs: Every time you resize a band, the cartridge layout has to be re-measured and re-approved in the assembler's repo - a deliberate act in a different project. It turns a normal art tweak into a cross-project chore, which cuts against the whole point of the effects work: that something you build in the editor just reaches the game.

recommend.because: It is the only option that costs you nothing at authoring time and does not spend the room you may want later. It also matches how this engine already handles the same kind of limit elsewhere - the number of bands is a declared ceiling with a guard that names it - so it is the consistent choice rather than a new idea. And the failure it produces is a sentence telling an author their band is too big, which is the failure you want if you are ever going to hit one.

detail: ojz_bg_anim's frozen allotment is 2 bytes (measured from the disabled stub: BgAnim_Table u16 = 0 plus Data.empty). Section size derives exactly as 46 + cols*rows*8*32 (2 + 12 + 32 header/record/pointer bytes + cols*rows*BANKS*32 bank blob); aurora's authored 8x4 band = 8238, matching the observed span [0x3B270,0x3D29E) exactly. Range over legal author geometries: 1x1=302, 8x4=8238, 16x8=32814, 32x14 (all 448 tiles)=114734. Slack before the hardware-pinned dac_banks anchor at 0x48000 is ~119 KB. Mechanism: native.rs:2947-2970 makes a section an anchor (Pinned) when its frozen true base exceeds the running chain end, so growth collides with the next pinned chain rather than flowing. Precedent for the ceiling shape: BGANIM_MAX_BANDS, a declared ceiling with a span guard (tools/test_bg_emit.py::TestBgAnimBandCeiling). Raised independently by the aurora lane (from band arithmetic) and this lane (from sigil's placement mechanism) - different enumeration parameters, so corroboration rather than echo.

question: Supersedes d-6, whose recommendation was wrong - I checked it against this project's own history and it fails there. The question is still how big to make the slot an animated background band lives in, but it now has an obvious answer. Reserving room for the biggest background animation that could ever exist turns out to cost nothing at all, because the space it would use is already an unused gap sitting in the middle of the cartridge, doing nothing, and it cannot be used by anything else. So the choice is really just: take the free room, or don't.

options.name: Reserve room for the largest animation that is physically possible
options.what: Every background animation an author could ever draw fits. No limit, no build failures, and this question never comes back. It fits with about 4 KB to spare.
options.costs: Nothing measurable. The cartridge does not grow - the space is an existing hole between two fixed points that nothing else can reach.

options.name: Reserve only enough for the animation this zone used to have
options.what: Restores what was lost and leaves a little headroom. Slightly less of the gap is claimed.
options.costs: An author who draws more animation than the zone originally had gets a build failure, and the leftover gap still cannot be used for anything else - so the saving is not real. You would be buying a future problem for nothing.

recommend.because: It is free. The space is a hole between the animation slot and a point in the cartridge that cannot move, so it is already wasted; claiming it for background animation costs nothing and removes an entire class of build failure permanently. My earlier recommendation of a smaller ceiling was wrong for two reasons the aurora lane caught: it was smaller than the animation this zone SHIPPED before it was deleted, and I had sized it per-band when the space actually holds every band added together.

detail: SUPERSEDES d-6. Two corrections from aurora, both verified firsthand here. (1) Per-band ceiling was the wrong unit: BgAnim_Banks is one blob for ALL bands in the act, so history's 32x4 + 16x4 both pass a 16x8 per-band ceiling while their sum (192 slots = 49,152 B) overflows a 32 KB allotment. (2) The historical content is real, not hypothetical: b0e5a661's editor_bg_override.json carries 32x4 + 16x4 / 8 phases = 192 slots, and games/sonic4/data/generated/ojz/act1/bg_anim_banks.bin is 49,152 bytes on disk right now (stale artifact the stub path never rewrote) - two independent sources, no shared step. Worst case is provably bounded: bands pack contiguously from slot 0 as a prefix of tiles (validate_band_coherence), so total slots <= BG_TILE_CAPACITY = 448 regardless of band count; max section = 2 + 44*BGANIM_MAX_BANDS(4) + 448*8*32 = 114,866. Slack check re-derived here rather than taken from the booking, because the booking's '~119 KB' subtracted only HeightMaps: the five shifting labels (Map_TestObj, Ani_Sonic, Ani_Tails, Ani_Particle, HeightMaps+Rot) pack into [0x27E72,0x2AEE0) and the free hole is AFTER them, [0x2AEE0,0x48000) = 119,072 B. Worst-case section from 0x27E70 plus the 12,398 B of shifted labels ends at 0x46F50, clearing the hardware-pinned dac_banks anchor at 0x48000 by 4,272 B. Interior hole = no ROM growth. Aurora's stated realistic bar was 49,152 ('can restore what was lost'); worst case dominates it at no cost. Note BG_BAND_RESERVE = 128 tiles / BG_STATIC_TILE_BUDGET = 320 is a separate authoring-side budget and is NOT this number.

question: Supersedes d-7. I told you reserving room for background animation was free. It is not - I read a gap in a table as empty space when it is actually full of Sonic's artwork, and I checked the ROM itself only afterwards. The corrected picture: the animation slot sits in a packed neighbourhood ending at a fixed hardware address that cannot move, and the only free room there is about 11 KB. Aurora's current band needs 8 KB and fits. The two-band animation this zone shipped before needs 49 KB and does not. So the real question is whether background animation stays small enough to live where it is, or gets moved somewhere with actual room.

options.name: Keep it where it is and accept a small ceiling
options.what: Aurora's band works now, this afternoon, with no layout upheaval. Background animation is capped at roughly one band of the size they drew.
options.costs: The two-band animation this zone used to have cannot be restored - it needs four times the room available. You would be choosing to leave that content deleted.

options.name: Move background animation somewhere with real room
options.what: Animation gets a home sized for whatever an author wants, including restoring the old two-band version and more. Removes the ceiling question permanently.
options.costs: A bigger, more careful change to how the cartridge is laid out, and it makes the ROM file grow rather than filling an existing gap. Slower - it is a proper parcel rather than a fix, and it touches the assembler project too.

options.name: Move Sonic's artwork instead and leave animation where it is
options.what: Frees around 97 KB right next to the animation slot, which covers almost any band.
options.costs: Sonic's artwork is the single biggest thing in that part of the cartridge and everything about how it loads is tuned around where it sits. Highest risk of the three for the least clear benefit. I do not recommend it and list it so you can see it was considered.

recommend.because: It unblocks aurora today with the band they already drew, and it is reversible - choosing it does not prevent moving animation later if you decide you want the old two-band version back. The relocation is the better end state but it should be a deliberate piece of work rather than something we rush into while aurora is waiting. Take the quick win, keep the bigger question open.

detail: RETRACTS the central premise of d-7 AND of the DEFERRED_WORK booking. All three of us (this lane, aurora, and the booking itself) read the [HeightMaps+0x2000, Dac_Temp_Blip) gap in the frozen boundary table as ~119,072 B of slack. It is not slack: s4.debug.lst lines 2225-2229 show AngleTable 0x2AEE0, SolidityTable 0x2AFE0, Map_Sonic 0x2B0E0, DPLC_Sonic 0x2CD60, Art_Sonic 0x2D6A0 filling it. Measured on the ROM: only 43.8% of that span is zero. THE BOOKING WARNED AGAINST THIS EXACT INFERENCE ('the golden table records BASES ONLY - a gap is an ALLOTMENT, never proven free space') and then committed it two paragraphs later on a different label pair; the frozen table is a BOUNDARY table listing a subset of labels, so gaps in it are invisible content, and only the .lst or the ROM can tell you which. Corrected free space, by constant-byte run scan of s4.debug.bin: the only real hole before the anchor is 0x4535D-0x48000 = 11,427 B (caveat: I have NOT established whether that tail is unowned or is trailing blank tiles belonging to Art_Sonic, so treat 11,427 as an upper bound and shape-specific - the plain shape will differ and the ceiling must be the MINIMUM across shapes). Against that: aurora's 8x4 band = 8,238 fits with ~3.2 KB spare; history's 32x4+16x4 = 49,242 does not; the provable worst case 114,866 is not close. Other holes found: 0x48B40-0x50000 = 29,888 (inside the DAC bank window, hardware-aligned, presumed unusable) and 0xAEC2-0x10000 = 20,798 (before the object code bank). Art_Sonic is ~97,469 B, consistent with this engine's uncompressed sprite art. EndOfRom 0xa3290 = 668,304 against a 715,010-byte debug file, so 'space after the end' means GROWING the ROM, not filling a hole - d-7's 'no ROM growth' claim does not survive either.

question: Same question as d-8 and the same answer from me - this only sharpens what option one costs, because the aurora lane closed a caveat I had left open. The 11 KB of room next to the animation slot is not spare: it is the breathing space at the end of Sonic's artwork. Using it for animation means Sonic's art has that much less room to grow into, and after Aurora's band fits there is about 3 KB left before a hardware address that cannot move.

options.name: Keep it where it is and accept a small ceiling
options.what: Aurora's band works today with no layout upheaval, and you can still move animation later if you change your mind - nothing is foreclosed.
options.costs: Spends most of the growing room at the end of Sonic's artwork and leaves about 3 KB of margin. The old two-band animation still cannot be restored. If Sonic's art ever grows, this has to be revisited.

options.name: Move background animation somewhere with real room
options.what: Animation gets a proper home, the old two-band version becomes restorable, Sonic's artwork keeps its growing room, and the ceiling question is gone for good.
options.costs: A careful layout change that makes the ROM file grow, touches the assembler project, and takes real time. Aurora waits longer.

recommend.because: Unchanged from d-8, and Aurora agrees: they would rather the move be done deliberately later than rushed to unblock them. Three KB of margin is thin but it is real, and nothing about taking it now prevents the relocation - you would be giving the space back, not undoing work. The honest summary is that this buys you weeks and costs you a little of Sonic's growing room. I dropped the third option from d-8 (moving Sonic's artwork instead); it was the highest risk for the least benefit and neither lane favours it.

detail: Detail-only in substance; filed as an entry because option 1's COSTS moved, which the contract's test makes an entry rather than a footnote. Aurora reproduced the whole d-8 measurement independently (43.8% zero to the decimal, 11,427 B run at 0x4535D) and closed the ownership caveat: the run begins at offset 97,469 into Art_Sonic, and 97,469 mod 32 = 29, so it is NOT a whole number of blank tiles - it is padding after the art, not indexed blank art. Verified here. Either way it sits inside Art_Sonic's allotment [0x2D6A0,0x48000), 89% of the way through, so the correct framing is 'shrinking what Sonic's art may grow into', not 'claiming unowned space'. Margin after an 8,238 B band shift: 11,427 - 8,238 = 3,189 B to the hardware-pinned dac_banks anchor. Aurora's judgement, which I share: treat 11,427 as hostile to depend on rather than as an upper bound, since Art_Sonic is the single most growth-prone object in this region. Aurora also owns having relayed the bad 119 KB figure onward twice and has corrected their owner.
